title: Hall's Marriage Theorem
quickIdea: Hall's condition is a counting guarantee: a matching that covers all of one side exists exactly when no group of vertices on that side is short of distinct neighbours.
remember: Hall's theorem: a matching saturating every vertex of L exists if and only if |N(S)| is at least |S| for every subset S of L.
The failure witness is one subset: if some S has fewer than |S| neighbours, those vertices must share too few partners, so one of them is left unmatched.
Defect form: the largest matching leaves at most max over S of (|S| - |N(S)|) vertices of L unmatched.
Checking every subset is exponential, but finding the matching is polynomial, by augmenting paths or by maximum flow with unit capacities.
A d-regular bipartite graph satisfies Hall, so it has a perfect matching, and its edges split into d perfect matchings.
Hall saturates one side; a perfect matching additionally needs the two sides to have equal size and Hall to hold in both directions.

example.prompt: L = {a, b, c}, R = {1, 2, 3}, with edges a-1, a-2, b-2, c-2, c-3. Is there a matching saturating L?
example.work: Check the tight subsets. N({a,b}) = {1,2} has size 2, N({b,c}) = {2,3} has size 2, N({a,c}) = {1,2,3} has size 3, and N(L) has size 3. Every subset meets Hall's bound, so a saturating matching exists: a-1, b-2, c-3.
example.answer: Yes: Hall's condition holds and a-1, b-2, c-3 saturates all of L.

gateAngle: GATE states Hall in words ('a complete matching exists if and only if every r vertices have at least r neighbours') and tests it through d-regular graphs. The exam form is almost always: find the one subset that breaks the condition.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: L = {a, b, c, d}, R = {1, 2, 3}, with edges a-1, b-1, c-2, d-2, d-3. Can a matching saturate L?
variations.answer: No. N({a,b}) = {1} has size 1, which is less than 2.
variations.why: Two left vertices have a single shared neighbour, so one of them must stay unmatched.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is checking only |N(L)| at least |L| not enough?
variations.answer: A smaller subset can be starved while the whole of L is not.
variations.why: Hall quantifies over every subset, and a small bottleneck inside L is invisible at the level of all of L.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A 4-regular bipartite graph has 20 vertices in total. How many edges does it have, and what matching is guaranteed?
variations.answer: 40 edges, from 20 x 4 / 2, and a perfect matching of 10 edges is guaranteed.
variations.why: A d-regular bipartite graph satisfies Hall, and with equal sides a saturating matching is perfect.

trap.what: Concluding 'no perfect matching' when the real failure is a Hall violation, or checking Hall only for the whole of L.
trap.why: Hall is an if-and-only-if for saturating L; a failure on a proper subset is the usual GATE trap, and it is also what the defect form measures.
trap.counterexample: L = {a,b,c}, R = {1,2,3} with a-1, b-1, c-1, c-2, c-3 has |N(L)| = 3 = |L| yet fails at S = {a,b}, where |N(S)| = 1.

check.question: L = {a, b, c}, R = {1, 2, 3}, with edges a-1, b-1, c-2, c-3. Does Hall's condition hold, and what is the maximum matching size?
check.answer: Hall fails at S = {a, b}, and the maximum matching has 2 edges.
check.explanation: N({a,b}) = {1} has size 1 against |S| = 2, so a and b cannot both be matched; the best is to match one of them to 1 and c to 2 or 3, giving 2 edges, and the defect form also reports 1 unmatched left vertex.

sources.title: Graph Theory: Connectivity, Coloring, Matching - GO Classroom slide deck
sources.note: slide text read through graph basics, walk/path/circuit, Euler and Hamiltonian, cut-set and cut-vertex, edge and vertex connectivity, colouring, bipartite, independent set, matching and Hall's theorem; the fetch was truncated after the Havel-Hakimi example, so the later matching pages were read only as excerpts

sourceLine: Hall's marriage theorem, the complete-matching condition and the d-regular corollary: GATE Overflow GO Classroom deck (English, read in part) for the complete-matching theorem in its r-subset form; West and the NPTEL IIITB lecture sequence (structure only) for the standard proof. Standard references used to verify, never copied: Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, ch. 10; West, Introduction to Graph Theory (Brooks, Dirac, Koenig, chromatic polynomial); CLRS ch. 22 (articulation points, bridges) and ch. 26 (bipartite matching); Diestel, Graph Theory (Menger). Hall's condition, the defect form and both examples are recomputed by brute force in scripts/validate.py.
